title: Words That Frame the News
text:
Headlines are rarely neutral. A single word chosen by an editor can frame an event as a triumph or a catastrophe, subtly steering readers toward a conclusion before they have read a single fact. Scholars of discourse analysis call this framing, and they argue that it operates most powerfully when it goes unnoticed. Consequently, media literacy begins with the habit of asking who chose the wording, and why.

Yet the same skepticism can be misapplied. Readers who assume every story is manufactured may dismiss accurate reporting simply because it is inconvenient to their existing beliefs. A more productive stance is to weigh the evidence a source provides, check whether its claims can be verified, and notice what it omits. Critical reading, in other words, demands vigilance without cynicism.

questions.text: According to the passage, what can a single word chosen by an editor do?
options: Frame an event as a triumph or a catastrophe
Remove all facts from a report

questions.text: What does the passage say readers may do when they assume every story is manufactured?
options: Dismiss accurate reporting that is inconvenient to them
Verify every claim with an expert
Read only the headlines of each story
Trust every source they come across

questions.text: Why does the author suggest that framing is most powerful when it goes unnoticed?
options: Because readers who do not notice it cannot easily question its influence
Because editors always intend to deceive their audiences
Because unnoticed framing is shorter than an explicit argument
Because scholars have proven that all headlines are false

questions.text: What is the author's implied attitude toward blanket cynicism about the media?
options: It is a misapplied form of skepticism that can also distort judgment
It is the only reliable way to read the news
It is an approach favored by professional discourse analysts
It is harmless because it never affects what people believe

vocabulary.definition: the way information is presented so as to shape how it is understood
in a way that is difficult to notice
careful attention to possible danger or error
a general distrust of other people's motives

paragraph_translations: As manchetes raramente são neutras. Uma única palavra escolhida por um editor pode apresentar um acontecimento como um triunfo ou uma catástrofe, orientando sutilmente os leitores a uma conclusão antes mesmo de lerem um único fato. Estudiosos da análise do discurso chamam isso de enquadramento e argumentam que ele funciona com mais força quando passa despercebido. Por isso, a alfabetização midiática começa com o hábito de perguntar quem escolheu a redação e por quê.

No entanto, o mesmo ceticismo pode ser mal aplicado. Leitores que presumem que toda notícia é fabricada podem rejeitar reportagens precisas simplesmente porque elas são inconvenientes para suas crenças. Uma postura mais produtiva é avaliar as evidências que uma fonte apresenta, verificar se suas afirmações podem ser comprovadas e notar o que ela omite. Em outras palavras, a leitura crítica exige vigilância sem cinismo.
